proposal.problem: A synthetic networking paper claims that adding 20 ms one-way delay changes TCP flow completion time (FCT) under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions. The magnitude of the change is described with a threshold value of '0.2', but the unit is disputed: the paper reportedly says seconds (0.2 s = 200 ms) while a user note says milliseconds (0.2 ms). The two values differ by a factor of 1000 and lead to entirely different falsification criteria. No full text or figure is available to resolve the ambiguity from metadata alone.
proposal.question: Under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, does adding 20 ms one-way delay produce a change in TCP FCT that exceeds 0.2 seconds (200 ms), or 0.2 milliseconds (0.2 ms), and which threshold is consistent with the paper's claim?
proposal.hypothesis: Under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, adding 20 ms delay changes TCP flow completion time.
proposal.conditions: Two delay conditions are tested: (A) baseline — 0 ms added one-way delay; (B) treatment — 20 ms added one-way delay. All other parameters (bottleneck rate, buffer, CCA, file size) are held fixed. Proposed defaults pending owner confirmation: bottleneck 10 Mbit/s, buffer 128 kbytes, CCA cubic, file size 10 MBytes, 0% loss. Both candidate thresholds (0.2 s and 0.2 ms) are evaluated as separate falsification bounds.
proposal.related_work: Source citation: 'Synthetic networking paper claim for development evaluation' (sha256: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa). Review status: retrieved-unreviewed. No full text provided; coverage is recorded metadata only. The unit ambiguity (seconds vs. milliseconds) cannot be resolved from available metadata.
proposal.alternatives: 1. The true threshold is 0.2 seconds (200 ms): plausible for large files or low-bandwidth bottlenecks where RTT inflation dominates. 2. The true threshold is 0.2 milliseconds (0.2 ms): plausible only if the claim refers to a sub-millisecond precision metric or a statistical bound, not a raw FCT difference. 3. The '0.2' figure refers to a normalized ratio or fraction, not an absolute time — this would require a different metric entirely. 4. The paper uses a different delay value or a different dependent variable than FCT.
proposal.design: Pilot experiment using the emulated-netem-v1 runner. Two client flows are run under each of the two delay conditions (0 ms and 20 ms). FCT is recorded in milliseconds for each flow. The mean FCT difference (treatment minus baseline) is computed and compared against both candidate thresholds: 200 ms (0.2 s) and 0.2 ms. Replications: 16 per condition (8 per condition per client, interleaved). Proposed bottleneck: 10 Mbit/s, 128 kbytes buffer, cubic CCA, 10 MBytes file, 0% loss. Owner must confirm or override bottleneck parameters and resolve the unit question before the protocol is frozen. This is a pilot; causal or generalizing conclusions are not warranted from a single emulated pilot.
proposal.metrics: Primary metric: flow_completion_time_ms (milliseconds). Derived metric: mean FCT difference between 20 ms delay condition and 0 ms baseline condition, in milliseconds. Both candidate falsification bounds are evaluated: (i) |ΔFCT| > 200 ms (0.2 s threshold); (ii) |ΔFCT| > 0.2 ms (0.2 ms threshold).
proposal.controls: Fixed across all runs: bottleneck rate, buffer size, CCA, file size, loss percentage (0%), number of clients (2), snapshot interval (100 ms). The only varied factor is added one-way client delay (0 ms vs. 20 ms). No other network parameters are changed between conditions.
proposal.falsification: The claim is not supported in this pilot if the observed mean FCT difference between the 20 ms delay condition and the 0 ms baseline is zero or negligible under both candidate thresholds. Specifically: (i) If |ΔFCT| ≤ 200 ms, the 0.2-second threshold is not exceeded; (ii) If |ΔFCT| ≤ 0.2 ms, the 0.2-millisecond threshold is not exceeded. Because the unit is unresolved, both bounds are evaluated and reported separately. A pilot result cannot establish causality or generalization. The unit ambiguity must be resolved by the owner using the original source before a definitive falsification rule is applied.
